How do we

02
Most of us…
🧑‍🏫listen to a teacher in history class,
📖read a book,
🎞️watch a documentary,
🗺️or perhaps go on a walking tour
to learn about the past.

We are given what historians already made for us.

03

But how do historians BEGIN to understand the past?

04

The past is a reconstruction. It is the retelling of a story using what evidence we can find…

and there is a LOT of evidence to look at.

05

Through this tool, we will look at just one way we can organise evidence:

Context

06

The process of building context is called contextualization.

It is the process of putting people, ideas, and events within their specific place and time…

then letting it shape our understanding of the past.

07

There are three main contexts to consider:

👤
Who?
Perspective — Who is the historical figure? What were they thinking?
🌍
Where?
Place — How did the place affect the perspective?
🕐
When?
Time — How did the time affect the perspective?
THEN…
AND…

drag THEN / AND — expand a lens to reveal it

09

Contextualisation is very important because we need it to make sense of a world we are no longer in– the past!

Context is not just putting people in random times and places.

When we paint a picture, it needs to make sense.

10

Now let's look at a claim relating to Stanford. If someone tells you…

Leland and Jane Stanford built the university in Palo Alto because it is located in Silicon Valley, a hub for the technology industry where their students can find the best opportunities.

Does this claim make sense?

11

Let's take a look at some evidence…

Why would this be a false statement? Provide your answer here (optional).

12

Stanford is indeed located in Silicon Valley.

But Silicon Valley as we know it today (even as a name) did not exist when Stanford was founded!

13

Leland and Jane Stanford founded this university in 1885. The first class graduated in 1895. The first “tech” company was not founded until 1939, which some call the beginning of Silicon Valley.

But even the beginning is debated! The term “Silicon Valley” did not even appear until 1971!

14

So no, Stanford was not founded for Silicon Valley. In fact, Silicon Valley was founded largely thanks to Stanford research.

Context helps us figure out how to make sense of the past.

15

Contextualisation is not only about what could have happened or not.

It is also used to help strengthen our explanations.

16

Now let's take a claim relating to Stanford and assess it with context…

17

When you picture Stanford, you probably picture engineering, research, business — an education built for the real world.

Today's top universities don't just teach theory; they focus on practical knowledge and real-world applications. Especially Stanford.

18

So here's a question: why does it even matter that Stanford was built to emphasize practical education?

Why does Stanford's Founding Grant name its goal as qualifying students for "personal success, and direct usefulness in life"?

Why is this important to recognise?
